analysis.one_liner: Creates a legal right to sue federal officials for violating your constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee, dying there about seven months later without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, if a state or local official violates your constitutional rights, federal law gives you a clear path to sue for damages. For federal officials, that right only exists because courts inferred it decades ago — and the Supreme Court has narrowed it sharply. This bill would amend that same federal law to explicitly let anyone sue federal officials, and recover money damages, when those officials violate their constitutional rights. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by federal officers — for example, someone subjected to an unlawful search, excessive force, or wrongful detention by a federal agent. The bill gives them an explicit, statutory right to sue that officer in court and recover damages, instead of depending on judicially created doctrines that courts have been steadily limiting.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the federal civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) so it covers officials acting under federal authority, not just state and local officials, giving victims an explicit statutory cause of action for damages.

Under current law, suits against federal officials for constitutional violations are only 'inferred' from the Constitution by court decisions, and the Supreme Court has limited where those suits are allowed; a statute would make the right to sue explicit rather than dependent on judicial doctrine.
The bill covers violations of constitutional rights generally — including due process and equal protection — by any person acting under federal authority, not a single agency.

analysis.who_pays: Federal officials and agencies that violate constitutional rights would face money damages in court. The federal government and its law-enforcement workforce bear the cost of expanded personal and institutional liability, which proponents argue is the point of accountability and opponents argue could chill aggressive enforcement.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of expanding civil liability for law enforcement argue that personal damages suits against officers can chill aggressive policing and national security work, and that questions of federal officer immunity should be set by courts rather than by statute; the bill takes no position on damage caps or qualified-immunity defenses, leaving key limits undefined.

The bill's text is a one-sentence amendment inserting 'of the United States or' into the statute; it does not spell out defenses, damages standards, or how cases against federal agencies would be handled, which a committee process would normally refine.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful but narrow: an explicit right to sue when a federal officer violates your constitutional rights, replacing a judge-made doctrine the Supreme Court has been shrinking. The cost falls on federal officers and agencies facing more lawsuits. The bill's brevity is its main design weakness — it changes one line of statute without addressing immunities or damages standards — so even supporters would need committee work to make it workable. It never got that chance.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, with Rep. Jamie Raskin as its cosponsor.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill's full action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal officers and agencies keep the status quo, where suing them for constitutional violations depends on narrow, judge-made doctrines rather than an explicit statute. People harmed by federal officer misconduct remain without the direct legal remedy the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an explicit statutory right to sue federal officials for constitutional violations.

for.name: Rep. Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor listed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill in the roughly seven months before Congress ended, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill; its two-record actions were introduction and committee referral.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and other federal officials
industries.note: The bill would expose federal officers and officials to damages suits for constitutional violations that courts have been narrowing away. Their interest in blocking it runs against the interest of people seeking redress for misconduct.
